spec.title: Offered vs accepted rate (k6)
spec.description: Offered = iterations started + dropped iterations. Accepted = 202 answers. They should overlap until the knee; after it accepted flattens while offered keeps rising. Compare the flat level with the Stage 1 value (about 1850 rps). Surprising: accepted below offered while latency is still low (then k6 or 503s are the cause, check row 4). k6 series are not marked stale after a run, so the last value can linger for minutes.

spec.title: Latency seen by k6: p50 / p99 / p99.9
spec.description: What the client sees. Flat then bends at the knee; the bend is the knee. Stage 1 was p99 about 10 ms below 1500 rps and over 1 s after the knee. Expect p50 above Stage 1 at low rates (batch wait of up to 5 ms plus the acks=all round trip). k6 trend is a native histogram (no _bucket series).

spec.title: Latency seen by the server: p50 / p99 (POST /v1/events)
spec.description: Server-side view of the same request. If this stays flat while k6 latency climbs, the wait is outside the handler (accept queue, k6 itself). Surprising: server p99 high while k6 p99 is low (cannot happen except for clock/bucket effects).

spec.title: Average batch size (messages per Kafka send)
spec.description: Messages per batch = roughly rate x (queue wait + send time). It grows with the rate. At the knee a flat batch size means the batcher is not the limit. The cap is BATCH_MAX_MESSAGES (500 default); touching it would be surprising.

spec.title: Batch flushes per second by reason
spec.description: Why each batch was sent: time (the 5 ms window), size (message or byte cap), drain (shutdown). Time flushes dominate at low rates; size flushes at high rates mean the cap is being hit.

spec.title: Time inside Kafka send: p50 / p99
spec.description: Time from handing a batch to the client until the broker acks (acks=all, 3 replicas). This is the part Kafka owns. Compare with the raw perf-test latency. It should stay flat; a rise means the brokers are saturating.

spec.title: Time waiting in the batcher queue: p50 / p99
spec.description: Time an event waits before its batch is sent. About the 5 ms window at low rates. A rise past the window means batches are waiting for a free in-flight slot (BATCH_MAX_IN_FLIGHT=1 default): the batcher, not Kafka, is the limit.

spec.title: Batcher queue depth and in-flight batches
spec.description: Queue depth should stay near zero below the knee. Growth means the batcher produces slower than requests arrive. Limit is BATCH_MAX_QUEUE (10000 default): reaching it makes the API answer 503.

spec.title: Broker round trip seen by the client (p50 / p99 per broker)
spec.description: librdkafka's own measure of request round trip per broker. A broker with a much higher value than the others is the slow one (the leader of a hot partition, or the most loaded CPU).

spec.title: Node process CPU (user vs system)
spec.description: CPU seconds per second used by the ingest-api process. The server is pinned to 2 logical CPUs (one core with SMT), so the maximum is 2.0. The event loop is one thread, so about 1.0 means the main thread is full. Compare user vs system: high system share means syscalls and socket work.

spec.title: Server cores busy (pinned CPUs, node_exporter)
spec.description: Busy share of each CPU the server is pinned to (1 - idle). 100% on one CPU while the other is lower means a single thread is the limit. Knee with this at about 100% = API CPU limit (the hypothesis).

spec.title: Broker cores busy (pinned CPUs, all 3 brokers share them)
spec.description: Busy share of the 4 CPUs the three brokers share (1,7,2,8 by default). This is broker CPU. A flat low value at the API knee shows Kafka is not the limit. Includes the broker JVMs only, because Postgres is moved off these CPUs by run.sh.

spec.title: Disk: bytes written per second (nvme0n1)
spec.description: Whole-disk write rate from node_exporter (not only Kafka: the host also writes). Brokers write the log and flush the page cache later, so writes arrive in bursts. A write rate near what the NVMe can sustain would make disk the limit, which would be surprising at these sizes.

spec.title: Event loop lag p99 (node)
spec.description: Delay of the node event loop. Near zero below the knee; rising to tens of ms is the main thread being saturated, which matches Node CPU about 1.0.

spec.title: Server heap used
spec.description: Heap used by node. Should be flat. Growth with rate would mean requests pile up in memory (queued messages).

spec.title: k6 dropped iterations (must be 0)
spec.description: Planned requests k6 could not start because no VU was free. Must stay 0 for a valid run. Above 0 means the generator (or a server too slow to answer) limits the test.

spec.title: Generator cores busy (k6 pinned CPUs)
spec.description: Busy share of the CPUs k6 is pinned to. Keep under about 70%. Above it the generator itself may be the limit: the hypothesis says the limit is API CPU or the generator, so this is the panel that separates them.

spec.title: k6 virtual users in use vs allowed
spec.description: VUs in use against the cap (MAX_VUS=3000). Using many more VUs than rate x latency means requests are slow. At the cap, k6 starts dropping iterations.

spec.title: Monitoring cores busy
spec.description: Busy share of the CPUs for Prometheus, Grafana and the idle Postgres. High means monitoring is disturbing the machine.

spec.title: API-side shedding: 503s and rejected events
spec.description: 503 answers by reason and events the batcher refused (queue full, breaker open). Must be 0 for a clean step; non-zero means the API protected itself, which is the real capacity limit.

spec.title: Kafka client health
spec.description: 1 = healthy / connected, breaker state 0 = closed (normal). A producer that disconnects or a breaker that opens during a run invalidates it.

2. The mechanism: where the time goes
3. Resource view: where the cost lands
4. Validity checks: can I trust this run?
